note: 'involuntarily' rendered as 'without resistance', which changes the sense.
replacement: Men in a state of nature are confined to what is physical in love. They are fortunate enough to be ignorant of those excellences which sharpen the appetite while they make it harder to satisfy. They must therefore be subject to fewer and less violent fits of passion, and so they fall into fewer and less violent quarrels. The imagination, which causes such ravages among us, never speaks to the heart of savages. They quietly await the impulses of nature and yield to them involuntarily, with more pleasure than ardor; and once their wants are satisfied, the desire is gone. It is therefore beyond dispute that love, like all the other passions, must have acquired in society that glowing impetuosity which so often makes it fatal to mankind. It is all the more absurd to portray savages as continually cutting one another's throats to indulge their brutality, because this opinion is directly contrary to experience. The Caribeans, who have so far deviated least of all from the state of nature, are in fact the most peaceable of people in their love affairs and the least subject to jealousy, though they live in a hot climate which seems always to inflame the passions.

note: Awkward dangling 'so let us conclude that' and 'fitting to'; the second 'let us conclude' is displaced.
replacement: Let us conclude, then, that man in a state of nature has no industry, no speech and no home, but wanders up and down the forests. He is as much a stranger to war as to every tie. He has no need of his fellow creatures and no desire to harm them, and perhaps does not even tell one from another. Let us conclude also that, being self-sufficient and subject to so few passions, he could have only such feelings and knowledge as befitted his situation. He felt only his actual necessities. He paid no attention to anything he did not think himself immediately concerned to notice, and his understanding advanced no further than his vanity. If he happened to make a discovery, he was the less able to pass it on, because he did not even know his own children. Every art would necessarily die with its inventor, where men had no kind of education and generation followed generation without the least advance. All started from the same point, and so centuries must have gone by in the barbarism of the first ages; the race was already old, and man remained a child.
